Healthcare Analytics: Risk-Stratified Outcomes and Forward Revenue Projection¶

Author: Olivia Cai · Date: May 2026

Tech stack: pandas, NumPy, scikit-learn, statsmodels, scipy, factor_analyzer, seaborn

TL;DR. A connected chain of techniques (data screening → PCA → K-Means → rule-based stratification → A/B testing → bootstrap + Monte Carlo) applied to a synthetic 100K-patient EHR cohort. Headline finding: high-risk patients (Charlson index ≥ 2, age ≥ 65) have 3.5x the 30-day readmission rate of low-risk patients (19.9% vs 5.7%, p < 1e-15, 95% CI on the gap [+10.7 pp, +17.6 pp]), but no statistically significant per-stay cost gap. The actionable lever is readmission, not cost.

Project Overview¶

This project analyzes a synthetic Electronic Health Records (EHR) dataset modeled on adult US patients from 2018 to 2024. The dataset is calibrated against CDC NHANES (vitals), CDC NCHS (disease prevalence), and CMS (hospitalization and readmission) benchmarks. The goal is to translate raw clinical data into actionable healthcare insights using a connected chain of statistical techniques.

Project flow:

  1. Screen and clean the data, then engineer clinically meaningful features.
  2. Merge the patients and outcomes datasets to focus on the 6,725 hospitalized patients that pass the data quality screen.
  3. Apply Principal Component Analysis (PCA) to test for latent structure in the patient feature space. KMO = 0.511 and 7 components needed for 69% cumulative variance, a documented diagnostic finding that this synthetic dataset has limited shared variance for PCA to consolidate.
  4. Apply K-Means clustering on the principal components. Silhouette peaks at 0.143 (problematic band) and the partition mostly recovers the engineered high_cost_flag rather than discovering distinct personas, so we pivot to a clinically-defined risk stratification (charlson_index >= 2 and age >= 65 for High, the inverse for Low, Medium otherwise), which produces a clean monotonic gradient on demographics, vitals, and outcomes.
  5. Use A/B testing (Welch's t-tests and two-proportion z-tests) on the rule-based strata to verify they differ on cost and readmission outcomes, identify confounders, and stratify on comorbidity_count to confirm robustness.
  6. Use bootstrap resampling to quantify uncertainty in our point estimates and Monte Carlo simulation to project forward to next year's revenue under a 10% volume-growth scenario.
  7. Translate the analytical findings into business recommendations.

The narrative moves from the broad population to outcome-linked patients to specific patient segments, covering both breadth and depth.

Decision on days_to_readmission: The 5,814 nulls correspond exactly to patients who were not readmitted within 30 days, so the NaN is structurally meaningful here. Imputing 0 here would conflate being readmitted on day zero (or the same day as leaving) with never being readmitted at all, and dropping the rows would discard the majority of the dataset. Therefore, we chose to preserve the NaN and use readmitted_30d for any readmission-rate analyses.

2.3 Outliers (IQR method)¶

We use the Tukey 1.5 x IQR rule to flag extreme values in each numerical column. A value is an outlier if it is below Q1 minus 1.5 x IQR or above Q3 plus 1.5 x IQR.

Justification to flag outliers: in healthcare, extreme values often represent the highest-risk patients we most want to study (very high BP, very long ICU stays, very high cost admissions). Trimming would discard signal. We therefore flag outliers but do not remove them, and where the tails are likely to distort means we will rely on medians or non-parametric methods.

In [19]:
# Reusable helper: count IQR-defined outliers for a list of numerical columns
def count_iqr_outliers(df, columns):
    """Return a DataFrame summarizing low and high IQR outliers per column."""
    rows = []
    for col in columns:
        Q1 = df[col].quantile(0.25)
        Q3 = df[col].quantile(0.75)
        IQR = Q3 - Q1
        lower = Q1 - 1.5 * IQR
        upper = Q3 + 1.5 * IQR
        low_count = (df[col] < lower).sum()
        high_count = (df[col] > upper).sum()
        rows.append({'column': col, 'low_outliers': low_count, 'high_outliers': high_count,
                     'lower_bound': lower, 'upper_bound': upper})
    return pd.DataFrame(rows)

Summary of outliers found:

  • total_charges_usd has 461 high outliers (high-acuity, high-cost stays we want to keep).
  • length_of_stay_days has 307 high outliers (long stays, the kind of stays that drive readmission risk).
  • icu_days has 152 high outliers (entirely matches the 152 ICU admissions, expected).
  • bmi, systolic_bp, diastolic_bp, heart_rate, temperature_f, charlson_index all have IQR outliers in the patient data, but these are physiological tail values consistent with a heterogeneous adult population.

We keep these rows but flag them mentally and report medians alongside means in later sections where skew matters.

# Physiological cross-check 1: systolic BP must be strictly greater than diastolic BP.
# Any row where systolic <= diastolic is medically impossible.
bp_issue_mask = patient_df['systolic_bp'] <= patient_df['diastolic_bp']
print(f'Rows with systolic_bp <= diastolic_bp: {bp_issue_mask.sum()}')

# Physiological cross-check 2: icu_days cannot exceed total length_of_stay_days
icu_issue_mask = outcome_df['icu_days'] > outcome_df['length_of_stay_days']
print(f'Rows with icu_days > length_of_stay_days: {icu_issue_mask.sum()}')

Rows with systolic_bp <= diastolic_bp: 1200
Rows with icu_days > length_of_stay_days: 51

2.6 Data quality decision¶

We found 1,200 BP-impossible rows (1.2% of patients) and 51 ICU-impossible rows (0.7% of outcomes). Our approach is to flag these rows rather than silently drop them at the source DataFrame, then exclude them from the primary analytical dataset when we merge in Section 4. Keeping a flagged copy lets us run a sensitivity analysis later if we want to confirm conclusions hold with or without the questionable rows.

In [32]:
# Create a binary data_quality_flag column on each source DataFrame.
# 1 means the row failed at least one integrity check, 0 means it passed.
patient_df['data_quality_flag'] = bp_issue_mask.astype(int)
outcome_df['data_quality_flag'] = icu_issue_mask.astype(int)

print(f"Patients flagged for BP issue: {patient_df['data_quality_flag'].sum()}")
print(f"Outcomes flagged for ICU/LOS issue: {outcome_df['data_quality_flag'].sum()}")

Patients flagged for BP issue: 1200
Outcomes flagged for ICU/LOS issue: 51

3. Feature Engineering¶

We engineer features that turn raw EHR fields into clinically interpretable risk indicators and analytically useful inputs. For every transformation we record the method and the reason it was chosen here, because the encoding choice changes what downstream models can and cannot learn.

3.1 Encode categorical variables¶

Feature Method Justification
gender Label encode (M=0, F=1) Binary nominal; with only two levels, label encoding is equivalent to one-hot with drop_first
smoking_status, alcohol_use, exercise_level Ordinal encode These are ranked behaviors with a natural intensity ordering, so the order carries information that PCA can exploit
insurance_type One-hot encode with drop_first=True Nominal with no inherent order; dropping the first level avoids perfect multicollinearity (the dummy variable trap) which would distort variance-based methods like PCA
In [33]:
# Label encode gender. Either direction is arbitrary; we use M=0, F=1 to match the
# order in the unique value list.
patient_df['gender'] = patient_df['gender'].map({'M': 0, 'F': 1})
In [34]:
# Ordinal encode the three lifestyle features.
# Order is fixed by clinical intensity (more = higher health risk for smoking/alcohol,
# more = lower risk for exercise but we still encode by intensity to keep direction
# consistent within each feature).
habit_maps = {
    'smoking_status':  {'never': 0, 'former': 1, 'current': 2},
    'alcohol_use':     {'none': 0, 'light': 1, 'moderate': 2, 'heavy': 3},
    'exercise_level':  {'sedentary': 0, 'light': 1, 'moderate': 2, 'vigorous': 3},
}
for col, mapping in habit_maps.items():
    patient_df[f'{col}_rank'] = patient_df[col].map(mapping)
In [35]:
# One-hot encode insurance_type. drop_first=True omits one dummy column so the remaining
# dummies are not perfectly collinear. Without this PCA would inflate the variance
# attributable to insurance and the design matrix would be rank-deficient for any
# regression-based downstream method.
patient_df = pd.get_dummies(patient_df, columns=['insurance_type'], drop_first=True)

3.2 Risk and severity features¶

In [36]:
# Comorbidity count: total number of chronic conditions per patient.
# Consolidates 15 sparse binary dx_ columns into one severity proxy that the model
# can weight as a single feature instead of fighting with 15 correlated indicators.
dx_cols = [col for col in patient_df.columns if col.startswith('dx_')]
patient_df['comorbidity_count'] = patient_df[dx_cols].sum(axis=1)
In [37]:
# Pulse pressure: systolic minus diastolic blood pressure.
# A clinically meaningful derived vital sign. High pulse pressure is an independent cardiovascular risk indicator separate from mean arterial pressure.
patient_df['pulse_pressure'] = patient_df['systolic_bp'] - patient_df['diastolic_bp']

3.3 Clinical binning of continuous features¶

We bin three continuous features (age, blood pressure, BMI) into clinically meaningful categories. The bin edges are not arbitrary, they come from established medical thresholds. Binning loses some precision but lets us run stratified analyses and produces ordinal features that combine well with the ordinal lifestyle ranks.

In [38]:
def assign_age_group(age):
    """Bin age into clinically meaningful groups. The 65 boundary aligns with US
    Medicare eligibility, which is a structural break in healthcare utilization."""
    if age < 40:
        return '<40'
    if age < 65:
        return '40-64'
    if age < 80:
        return '65-79'
    return '80+'


# Apply to all patients
patient_df['age_group'] = patient_df['age'].apply(assign_age_group)
patient_df['age_group'].value_counts()

def assign_bp_category(sys_bp, dia_bp):
    """American Heart Association blood pressure categories. Crisis is medically urgent."""
    if sys_bp >= 180 or dia_bp >= 120:
        return 'Crisis'
    if sys_bp >= 140 or dia_bp >= 90:
        return 'Stage_2_HTN'
    if sys_bp >= 130 or dia_bp >= 80:
        return 'Stage_1_HTN'
    if sys_bp >= 120:
        return 'Elevated'
    return 'Normal'


# Apply row-wise: needs both systolic and diastolic so we use a lambda over the row.
patient_df['bp_category'] = patient_df.apply(
    lambda r: assign_bp_category(r['systolic_bp'], r['diastolic_bp']), axis=1)
patient_df['bp_category'].value_counts()

def assign_bmi_category(bmi):
    """WHO BMI categories."""
    if bmi < 18.5:
        return 'Underweight'
    if bmi < 25:
        return 'Normal'
    if bmi < 30:
        return 'Overweight'
    if bmi < 40:
        return 'Obese'
    return 'Severely_Obese'

5. Principal Component Analysis (PCA)¶

Why PCA, when to use it: PCA is a linear dimensionality reduction technique that re-expresses a set of correlated features as a smaller set of uncorrelated components (the principal components, or PCs) ordered by the variance they explain. We use PCA here because the patient feature set is wide (age, BMI, two BP measurements, heart rate, temperature, pulse pressure, several lifestyle ranks, two severity scores, and several cost features) and many of these features are correlated. PCA condenses that into 3 or 4 somewhat interpretable latent dimensions that we then feed into clustering.

When PCA is not appropriate:

  • When original-feature interpretability is critical for the audience (PCs are weighted combinations).
  • When the features are mostly binary or have non-linear relationships (PCA captures only linear variance).
  • When the data is essentially uncorrelated. We verify this is not the case using KMO and Bartlett's test below.

5.1 Feature selection for PCA¶

We include continuous and ordinal features that describe patient state, health behavior, severity, and cost intensity. We exclude the 15 raw dx_ binaries because their information is already captured by comorbidity_count and charlson_index. We also exclude the one-hot insurance dummies because nominal indicators inflate dimensionality without contributing to a continuous latent factor.

In [47]:
# Feature list for PCA. Mix of continuous (age, bmi, BP, vitals) and ordinal (habit ranks).
pca_features = [
    'age', 'bmi', 'systolic_bp',
    'diastolic_bp',
    'pulse_pressure',
    'heart_rate', 'temperature_f',
    'charlson_index', 'comorbidity_count',
    'smoking_status_rank', 'alcohol_use_rank', 'exercise_level_rank',
    # 'length_of_stay_days', # Excluded based on very low KMO < 0.3
    'total_charges_usd', 'daily_charge',
]

# Drop rows with any nulls in the selected features. Should be zero given our cleaning.
pca_input = merged_df[pca_features].dropna().copy()
print(f'PCA input shape: {pca_input.shape}')

PCA input shape: (6725, 14)

5.2 Standardize¶

PCA decomposes the covariance matrix. Without scaling, features with large numeric range (total_charges_usd ranges over tens of thousands) would dominate features with small range (bmi ranges over tens), and the first PC would essentially be the cost axis. StandardScaler rescales each feature to mean 0 and standard deviation 1 so every feature gets a fair chance to load on each PC.

In [48]:
# Fit and apply the z-score scaler. The output is a numpy array of standardized values.
scaler = StandardScaler()
pca_scaled = scaler.fit_transform(pca_input)

# Wrap back in a DataFrame so column names survive for downstream interpretation.
pca_scaled_df = pd.DataFrame(pca_scaled, columns=pca_features, index=pca_input.index)
pca_scaled_df.describe().round(2)   # means ~0, std ~1 confirm scaling worked

5.3 Multicollinearity check via Variance Inflation Factor (VIF)¶

VIF measures how much the variance of each feature is inflated by its correlation with the other features in the matrix. A VIF of 1 means the feature is uncorrelated with the rest; VIF between 1 and 5 is moderate; greater than 5 is high; greater than 10 is severe. High VIF strengthens the case for PCA because PCA is designed to consolidate redundant correlated features.

In [49]:
def compute_vif(X, feature_names):
    """Return a tidy DataFrame of variance inflation factors, sorted descending.

    Parameters
    ----------
    X : array-like of shape (n_samples, n_features)
        Already standardized feature matrix.
    feature_names : list of str
        Names matching the columns of X.
    """
    rows = []
    X = np.asarray(X)
    for i, name in enumerate(feature_names):
        rows.append({'feature': name, 'VIF': variance_inflation_factor(X, i)})
    return pd.DataFrame(rows).sort_values('VIF', ascending=False).reset_index(drop=True)


vif_df = compute_vif(pca_scaled, pca_features)

Interpretation: The inf values for systolic_bp, diastolic_bp, and pulse_pressure indicate perfect multicollinearity, which is expected since pulse pressure is a direct mathematical derivative of the other two. While this level of redundancy would typically require dropping features in a standard regression, we will retain them here as Principal Component Analysis (PCA) is specifically designed to consolidate such highly correlated variables into meaningful latent dimensions. All other features show low VIF scores (generally < 2.5), suggesting they mostly contribute independent information to the model.

5.4 Pre-PCA suitability tests: KMO and Bartlett's sphericity¶

Before running PCA, we verify the data is actually suitable for dimensionality reduction. If features are essentially uncorrelated, PCA has nothing to compress.

Bartlett's test of sphericity:

  • H0: the correlation matrix is the identity (all off-diagonal correlations are 0).
  • H1: at least some features are correlated.
  • We need to reject H0 (small p-value, typically < 0.05) for PCA to be appropriate.

Kaiser-Meyer-Olkin (KMO): an overall measure of shared structure between 0 and 1.

Interpretation usually bands:

  • 0.90 to 1.00: Marvelous (Excellent)
  • 0.80 to 0.89: Meritorious (Very Good)
  • 0.70 to 0.79: Middling (Good/Acceptable)
  • 0.60 to 0.69: Mediocre (Barely Acceptable)
  • 0.50 to 0.59: Miserable (Poor)
  • Below 0.50: unacceptable, drop low-KMO features and re-check
In [50]:
def check_pca_suitability(X_scaled, feature_names):
    """Run Bartlett's sphericity test and KMO on a scaled feature matrix.

    Returns a dict with the chi-square, p-value, per-variable KMO Series,
    and the overall KMO score.
    """
    chi_sq, p_value = calculate_bartlett_sphericity(X_scaled)
    kmo_per_var, kmo_overall = calculate_kmo(X_scaled)
    return {
        'bartlett_chi_square': chi_sq,
        'bartlett_p_value': p_value,
        'kmo_per_variable': pd.Series(kmo_per_var, index=feature_names).sort_values(),
        'kmo_overall': kmo_overall,
    }


suitability = check_pca_suitability(pca_scaled, pca_features)

print(f"Bartlett p-value:    {suitability['bartlett_p_value']:.4g}")
print(f"KMO overall:         {suitability['kmo_overall']:.3f}")
print('KMO per variable (ascending):')
print(suitability['kmo_per_variable'].round(3))

Interpreting the KMO and Bartlett results.

  • Bartlett's test: the chi-square statistic of 250,410 with a p-value of 0 (i.e., far below 0.05) lets us reject the identity-correlation null. There is shared variance in the matrix, so PCA is not running on noise.
  • KMO overall = 0.511. This sits in the "miserable" band (0.50 to 0.60). Bartlett tells us some correlation exists; KMO tells us the amount of shared variance is small. A KMO this low forecasts what we are about to see: many components will be needed to capture a modest cumulative variance share, and component interpretability will be weaker than usual.

We proceed with PCA because the test is not unacceptable (above 0.50), but we treat the components as a diagnostic axis rather than a strong basis for downstream modeling, and we will pivot to clinically-defined patient segments in Section 6.5 for the A/B and simulation work.

5.5 Fit PCA and select the number of components¶

In [51]:
def run_pca(X_scaled, n_components=None, seed=RANDOM_SEED):
    """Fit PCA on a standardized matrix and return the fitted estimator plus scores.

    n_components=None fits a full PCA so we can inspect eigenvalues and pick K downstream.
    """
    pca = PCA(n_components=n_components, random_state=seed)
    scores = pca.fit_transform(X_scaled)
    return pca, scores


# Fit full PCA first so we can inspect every eigenvalue and variance explained.
pca_full, scores_full = run_pca(pca_scaled, n_components=None)

# explained_variance_ are eigenvalues; explained_variance_ratio_ is share of total variance.
explained_var = pd.DataFrame({
    'PC': [f'PC{i+1}' for i in range(len(pca_full.explained_variance_))],
    'eigenvalue': pca_full.explained_variance_,
    'variance_ratio': pca_full.explained_variance_ratio_,
    'cumulative_variance': np.cumsum(pca_full.explained_variance_ratio_),
})
explained_var.round(4)

5.6 Choosing the number of components¶

Interpreting the three component-selection criteria for this dataset.

  1. Kaiser criterion (eigenvalue > 1): retains 7 components. This is unusually many; a clean PCA application usually has 3 to 5 eigenvalues above 1.
  2. Scree elbow: the inflection point sits around PC4. After PC4 the eigenvalue curve flattens, with PCs 5 through 7 each barely clearing the eigenvalue = 1 threshold.
  3. Cumulative variance: 7 components are needed to reach 69.04%, just shy of the 70% target. PC1 through PC4 together capture only ~47%.

What this means: the criteria disagree, which itself is the finding. Kaiser is permissive here because so many features are essentially independent that each contributes its own eigenvalue near 1. The scree elbow at PC4 with under 50% variance is a more honest summary. We retain Kaiser's 7 components for completeness in Section 5.7's loadings interpretation, but we acknowledge that PCs 5 to 7 carry very limited information and the dataset does not have a strong low-dimensional structure for clustering to exploit.

In [53]:
# Set N_COMPONENTS based on the diagnostics above. Adjust after inspecting the plots.

print(f'Components retained by Kaiser rule: {N_COMPONENTS}')
print(f"Cumulative variance retained: {explained_var.iloc[N_COMPONENTS-1]['cumulative_variance']:.2%}")

Attempting PC Interpretation:

  • PC1: Vascular pressure and aging. Loads strongest on systolic_bp (0.59), pulse_pressure (0.56), age (0.37), and comorbidity_count (0.36). This captures the classic vascular aging signal: older patients with elevated systolic pressure and a widened systolic-diastolic gap, accompanied by greater chronic disease burden.
  • PC2: Diastolic-dominant chronic burden. Loads on diastolic_bp (0.46), comorbidity_count (0.43), charlson_index (0.35), and age (0.32), with a strong negative loading on pulse_pressure (-0.43). Patients high on PC2 show elevated diastolic pressure with a narrow pressure gap plus high comorbidity. This isolates a different cardiovascular phenotype from PC1: earlier-stage hypertension with chronic disease, rather than later-stage vascular stiffening.
  • PC3: Cost and utilization. Loads almost entirely on total_charges_usd (0.65) and daily_charge (0.64), with mild negative loadings on comorbidity_count (-0.24) and charlson_index (-0.22). This is a near-pure cost axis. The slight negative comorbidity loading is worth noting: it suggests the highest-cost stays in this dataset tend to be acute, single-episode admissions rather than chronic-disease driven stays.
  • PC4: Isolated hypertension without comorbidity. Loads on diastolic_bp (0.58), age (0.37), and systolic_bp (0.32) on the positive side, and strongly negatively on charlson_index (-0.55) and comorbidity_count (-0.30). Patients high on PC4 are older with elevated blood pressure but few documented comorbidities, an "isolated hypertensive" or possibly under-diagnosed phenotype.
  • PC5: Metabolic and inflammatory state. Loads on bmi (0.59), temperature_f (0.50), heart_rate (0.42), and smoking_status_rank (0.34), with a small negative on exercise_level_rank (-0.24). A metabolic-inflammatory axis: higher BMI, slightly elevated temperature and resting heart rate, more smoking, less exercise.
  • PC6: Smoking phenotype with bradycardia (slow heart rate). Loads on smoking_status_rank (0.56) and temperature_f (0.43) positive, and on heart_rate (-0.55) and bmi (-0.38) negative. The combination of heavy smoking with a low resting heart rate is somewhat unusual; in real-world data this often reflects long-term smokers on rate-lowering medications such as beta-blockers, but in a synthetic dataset it may simply be a residual axis after PC5 absorbs most of the metabolic signal.
  • PC7: Active drinker lifestyle. Loads on alcohol_use_rank (0.70) and exercise_level_rank (0.60), with a smaller positive on heart_rate (0.33) and a slight negative on bmi (-0.21). Captures a lifestyle pattern where high alcohol consumption co-occurs with high physical activity, suggestive of a younger or more socially active subset rather than a clinical risk axis.

5.8 Tradeoffs to consider¶

  • PCs are weighted combinations of original features, so we lose direct interpretability. We mitigate by naming each PC using its dominant loadings.
  • PCA only captures linear structure. For non-linear patterns t-SNE or UMAP (visualization) or kernel PCA (analysis) are alternatives.
  • PCA is sensitive to outliers because variance is a squared metric. Mitigation: remove extreme outliers, or use robust PCA.
  • PCA assumes features are at least roughly continuous. Forcing many binary features through PCA tends to produce uninformative components.

6. Clustering¶

Why clustering, when to use it: unsupervised segmentation when we want to discover natural groupings without a labeled target. Useful in healthcare for cohort discovery, risk stratification, and intervention targeting. The principal components from Section 5 are an ideal input because they are decorrelated, standardized, and low-dimensional.

Why K-Means specifically: fast on thousands of rows, easy to communicate to a non-technical stakeholder, and works well when clusters are roughly spherical in the reduced PC space.

6.1 Choose the number of clusters¶

In [56]:
def choose_k(X, k_range=range(2, 11), seed=RANDOM_SEED):
    """Run K-Means for each k in k_range, returning inertia and silhouette score.

    Inertia (within-cluster sum of squares) drives the elbow plot.
    Silhouette score in [-1, 1] measures how well-separated the clusters are.
    """
    rows = []
    for k in k_range:
        km = KMeans(n_clusters=k, n_init=10, random_state=seed)
        labels = km.fit_predict(X)
        rows.append({
            'k': k,
            'inertia': km.inertia_,
            'silhouette': silhouette_score(X, labels),
        })
    return pd.DataFrame(rows)


k_diag = choose_k(pc_scores, k_range=range(2, 11))

Interpreting the elbow and silhouette together.

The elbow plot has no clear inflection: inertia declines gently and continuously from k = 2 to k = 10, which is the visual signature of a dataset without natural geometric gaps between clusters.

The silhouette score is more diagnostic. It peaks at k = 3 with a value of 0.143, then declines as k grows. Using standard interpretation bands (0.71+ strong, 0.51 to 0.70 reasonable, 0.26 to 0.50 weak, 0.25 or below problematic), a peak of 0.143 falls clearly inside the problematic band. This means even the best K-Means partition we can build here has very weak cluster separation: most points are roughly equidistant from their own centroid and the nearest neighboring centroid.

We proceed with k = 3 to demonstrate the technique and produce the per-sample silhouette plot below, but we treat the resulting cluster labels as exploratory rather than as a basis for downstream inference. Section 6.5 introduces a clinically-defined segmentation that replaces the K-Means cluster labels for the A/B tests and simulations.

In [59]:
def run_kmeans(X, k, seed=RANDOM_SEED):
    """Fit KMeans with multiple inits and return both the fitted model and the labels."""
    km = KMeans(n_clusters=k, n_init=10, random_state=seed)
    labels = km.fit_predict(X)
    return km, labels


kmeans_model, cluster_labels = run_kmeans(pc_scores, K_FINAL)

def plot_silhouette(X, labels, k):
    """Per-sample silhouette plot colored by cluster. Reveals whether *every* cluster
    is well-formed, which the scalar silhouette_score cannot show."""
    sample_sils = silhouette_samples(X, labels)
    overall = silhouette_score(X, labels)

    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 6))
    y_lower = 10
    for i in range(k):
        cluster_sils = np.sort(sample_sils[labels == i])
        size_i = cluster_sils.shape[0]
        y_upper = y_lower + size_i
        color = cm.nipy_spectral(float(i) / k)
        ax.fill_betweenx(np.arange(y_lower, y_upper),
                         0, cluster_sils,
                         facecolor=color, edgecolor=color, alpha=0.7)
        ax.text(-0.05, y_lower + 0.5 * size_i, str(i))
        y_lower = y_upper + 10

    ax.axvline(overall, color='red', linestyle='--',
               label=f'Overall silhouette = {overall:.3f}')
    ax.set_xlabel('Silhouette coefficient')
    ax.set_ylabel('Sample (grouped by cluster)')
    ax.set_title(f'Per-sample silhouette plot (k = {k})')
    ax.legend()
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()


plot_silhouette(pc_scores, cluster_labels, K_FINAL)

6.3 Profile each cluster¶

For each cluster we compute average values of the outcome metrics and patient characteristics that matter most for healthcare decisions. The profile is what lets us name each cluster (e.g., high-acuity seniors vs healthy young adults).

Interpreting the K-Means cluster profile.

The profile table and heatmap reveal the structural problem behind the 0.143 silhouette. The three clusters K-Means produced are:

  • Cluster 0: youngest (mean age 70.8), lowest comorbidity (2.93), borderline Stage 1 hypertension by the AHA classifier we built in Section 3.3 (124/87, driven by the diastolic), moderate cost (~$15,000), 19% high-cost flag.
  • Cluster 1: oldest (mean age 83.8), highest comorbidity (4.23), Stage 2 systolic hypertension by the AHA classifier (149/...), similar moderate cost (~$15,000), 19% high-cost flag.
  • Cluster 2: middle on demographics (age 78.8, comorbidity 3.64) but dramatically higher cost (mean $58,953, mean daily charge $26,996, 100% high-cost flag).

In other words, Clusters 0 and 1 differ only on age and comorbidity but are nearly identical on cost and outcomes, and Cluster 2 is essentially the high-cost stays. The K-Means partition is mostly recovering the high_cost_flag we already engineered, not discovering distinct patient personas. That is a meaningful negative finding but also a clear signal that the segmentation we want for downstream A/B testing needs to come from somewhere else, which is the motivation for Section 6.5.

6.4 Tradeoffs to consider¶

  • K-Means assumes roughly spherical clusters of similar size. It struggles with elongated, nested, or unequal-size clusters.
  • K must be specified up front. We address this with elbow and silhouette diagnostics, but the choice still has a subjective element.
  • K-Means is sensitive to initialization. n_init=10 re-runs with different seeds and keeps the best, mitigating this.
  • Alternatives: hierarchical clustering (no K up front, dendrogram is interpretable, but O(n^2) memory), DBSCAN (finds arbitrary shapes and labels noise, but needs eps tuning), Gaussian Mixture Models (soft assignments and elliptical clusters).

6.5 Pivot to clinically-defined segments¶

The diagnostics above (KMO = 0.511, 7 PCs for 69% variance, silhouette of 0.143) tell us this dataset does not support a clean unsupervised segmentation. Rather than force K-Means to assign labels that the silhouette score says we should not trust, we segment patients using a clinically-justified rule and use that segmentation as the basis for the A/B tests and simulations that follow.

Rule we apply: combine charlson_index (the standard mortality risk proxy) with age (the dominant driver of healthcare utilization in the US, with the structural 65+ Medicare break). Patients who are both older and have meaningful comorbidity burden are the classic high-risk population that care-transition and chronic-disease management programs target.

  • High risk: charlson_index >= 2 and age >= 65. Older patients with moderate to severe comorbidity burden.
  • Low risk: charlson_index < 2 and age < 65. Younger patients with low comorbidity burden.
  • Medium risk: everyone else (older but lower comorbidity, or younger but higher comorbidity).

This rule is unsupervised in the sense that we did not learn it from the outcome variables, so it does not bias the downstream A/B tests, but it is clinically motivated rather than algorithmically discovered.

In [63]:
# Define the rule-based risk stratum function.
def assign_risk_stratum(charlson, age):
    """Classify a patient into a clinical risk stratum.

    High:   charlson_index >= 2 and age >= 65 (classic high-risk profile)
    Low:    charlson_index < 2 and age < 65 (younger, low-comorbidity)
    Medium: everyone else (one risk factor present but not both)
    """
    if charlson >= 2 and age >= 65:
        return 'High'
    if charlson < 2 and age < 65:
        return 'Low'
    return 'Medium'


# Apply row-wise to the merged DataFrame so each hospital stay gets a risk label.
merged_df['risk_stratum'] = merged_df.apply(
    lambda r: assign_risk_stratum(r['charlson_index'], r['age']), axis=1)

# Inspect the size of each stratum.
merged_df['risk_stratum'].value_counts()

Interpretation of the rule-based segments: the heatmap shows the clean monotonic gradient we wanted across nearly every clinically meaningful row, confirming that the rule-based stratification is recovering real structure that K-Means missed.

By construction, the three engineering-input rows climb steadily: age goes 51.24 to 78.32 to 83.86 (a 33-year gap from Low to High), comorbidity_count goes 2.21 to 3.27 to 4.48, and charlson_index goes 0.42 to 0.72 to 2.49, with the largest jump at the Medium-to-High boundary reflecting the charlson >= 2 threshold in the rule.

More importantly, the vital signs and outcomes track that gradient even though they were not used to define the strata. systolic_bp rises from 126.91 to 139.49, diastolic_bp from 79.70 to 86.87, and pulse_pressure from 47.22 to 52.62. These are emergent gradients, meaning the strata capture real cardiovascular risk progression on top of the age and comorbidity axis used to build them.

The outcome rows that will be used in the A/B tests of Section 7 show meaningful gradients too. readmitted_30d is the standout signal: 5.7% in Low, 13% in Medium, 19.9% in High, a 3.5x increase from Low to High. This is the kind of effect size that a two-proportion z-test should reject the null on decisively, and it points to a clear business case for a care-transition intervention targeting the High-risk stratum. icu_admission and in_hospital_death both climb from near-zero in Low to 2% in High, monotonic but with small absolute differences. daily_charge rises about 14% ($5,538 to $6,337), while total_charges_usd rises a more muted ~5.7% ($17,665 to $18,673), suggesting that intensity of care per day tracks risk better than total cost per stay on this dataset.

Two rows are nearly flat and worth flagging explicitly:

  • length_of_stay_days is essentially constant (5.22, 5.27, 5.26), implying that LOS is driven by other factors (DRG mix, discharge disposition) rather than by chronic risk.
  • high_cost_flag is not monotonic (0.25, 0.24, 0.26), which is striking. Top-quartile cost stays occur at the same rate across every risk stratum. This is consistent with PC3 in your PCA showing a negative loading of cost on comorbidity: high-cost outliers in this dataset are driven by acute, single-episode events (think a costly procedure or unplanned ICU stay) rather than by chronic disease burden.

7. A/B Testing¶

Why A/B testing here: our risk-based segmentation told us patient personas exist, but it cannot tell us whether the personas differ in outcomes that the business cares about. Hypothesis tests answer that. We define explicit null and alternative hypotheses, choose the appropriate test by outcome type (continuous mean vs binary proportion), and discuss confounders.

Test selection rule:

  • Continuous outcome (cost, length of stay) -> two-sample t-test (scipy.stats.ttest_ind with equal_var=False for Welch's adjustment).
  • Binary outcome (readmitted, mortality) -> two-proportion z-test (statsmodels.stats.proportion.proportions_ztest).
  • Multi-level categorical association -> chi-square test of independence (scipy.stats.chi2_contingency).

7.1 Reusable test functions¶

In [67]:
def cohen_d(a, b):
    """Cohen's d effect size for two independent samples. Pooled standard deviation."""
    a = np.asarray(a)
    b = np.asarray(b)
    pooled_sd = np.sqrt(((a.var(ddof=1) * (len(a) - 1)) +
                         (b.var(ddof=1) * (len(b) - 1))) / (len(a) + len(b) - 2))
    return (a.mean() - b.mean()) / pooled_sd if pooled_sd > 0 else np.nan


def test_means(group_a, group_b, alpha=0.05, alternative='two-sided'):
    """Welch's two-sample t-test wrapper.

    Parameters
    ----------
    group_a, group_b : array-like
        Samples from the two groups being compared.
    alpha : float
        Significance level for the reject/fail-to-reject decision.
    alternative : str
        'two-sided', 'greater', or 'less'.
        e.g. 'greater' means that Group A has a greater/higher mean than Group B.
    """
    a = np.asarray(group_a)
    b = np.asarray(group_b)
    t_stat, p_value = ttest_ind(a, b, equal_var=False, alternative=alternative)
    return {
        'test': "Welch's two-sample t-test",
        'alternative': alternative,
        'n_a': len(a),
        'n_b': len(b),
        'mean_a': a.mean(),
        'mean_b': b.mean(),
        'mean_diff': a.mean() - b.mean(),
        't_stat': t_stat,
        'p_value': p_value,
        'cohen_d': cohen_d(a, b),
        'reject_H0': p_value < alpha,
    }
In [68]:
def test_proportions(success_a, n_a, success_b, n_b, alpha=0.05, alternative='two-sided'):
    """Two-proportion z-test wrapper using statsmodels proportions_ztest.

    Parameters
    ----------
    success_a, success_b : int
        Number of successes (count of 1s) in each group.
    n_a, n_b : int
        Total sample size of each group.
    alternative : str
        'two-sided', 'greater', or 'less'. statsmodels uses 'larger'/'smaller'
        internally; we translate so the API matches test_means.
    """
    statsmodels_alt = {'two-sided': 'two-sided',
                       'greater': 'larger',
                       'less': 'smaller'}[alternative]
    counts = np.array([success_a, success_b])
    nobs = np.array([n_a, n_b])
    z_stat, p_value = proportions_ztest(counts, nobs, alternative=statsmodels_alt)
    p_a = success_a / n_a
    p_b = success_b / n_b
    return {
        'test': 'Two-proportion z-test',
        'alternative': alternative,
        'n_a': n_a,
        'n_b': n_b,
        'p_a': p_a,
        'p_b': p_b,
        'risk_diff': p_a - p_b,
        'z_stat': z_stat,
        'p_value': p_value,
        'reject_H0': p_value < alpha,
    }
In [69]:
def test_categorical_association(df, col_a, col_b, alpha=0.05):
    """Chi-square test of independence between two categorical columns.

    Used when a candidate confounder has more than 2 levels (e.g., insurance_type).
    """
    table = pd.crosstab(df[col_a], df[col_b])
    chi2, p_value, dof, expected = chi2_contingency(table)
    return {
        'test': 'Chi-square test of independence',
        'col_a': col_a,
        'col_b': col_b,
        'chi2': chi2,
        'dof': dof,
        'p_value': p_value,
        'reject_H0': p_value < alpha,
        'min_expected': expected.min(),   # check >= 5 assumption
    }

7.2 Test 1: Cost between the highest-risk and lowest-risk clusters¶

Rationale: if cost differs significantly between clusters, the high-cost cluster is the natural target for cost-reduction interventions. The size of the difference, not just the p-value, drives the business case.

  • H0: mean total_charges_usd is equal between the two clusters being compared.
  • H1: mean total_charges_usd differs (two-sided), or is greater in the high-risk cluster (one-sided).

7.3 Test 2: Readmission rate between the two clusters¶

  • H0: the 30-day readmission proportion is equal between the two clusters.
  • H1: the readmission proportions differ.

The risk difference is 0.1415 (14.15 percentage points), meaning the high-risk group has a substantially higher chance of readmission within 30 days compared to the low-risk group.

7.4 Confounder identification panel¶

A confounder is a third variable that differs between the two groups and is plausibly associated with the outcome. To make this empirical rather than hand-wavy, we test each candidate confounder for between-cluster difference.

In [74]:
def confounder_panel(df, group_col, group_a, group_b, continuous_cols=None,
                     binary_cols=None, categorical_cols=None, alpha=0.05):
    """Loop over candidate confounders and run the right test for each.

    Returns a tidy DataFrame summarizing test, statistic, p-value, decision.
    """
    continuous_cols = continuous_cols or []
    binary_cols = binary_cols or []
    categorical_cols = categorical_cols or []
    sub_a = df[df[group_col] == group_a]
    sub_b = df[df[group_col] == group_b]
    rows = []

    for col in continuous_cols:
        r = test_means(sub_a[col].dropna(), sub_b[col].dropna(), alpha=alpha)
        rows.append({'confounder': col, 'test': 'Welch t',
                     'statistic': r['t_stat'], 'p_value': r['p_value'],
                     'reject_H0': r['reject_H0']})

    for col in binary_cols:
        a_succ = int(sub_a[col].sum())
        b_succ = int(sub_b[col].sum())
        r = test_proportions(a_succ, len(sub_a), b_succ, len(sub_b), alpha=alpha)
        rows.append({'confounder': col, 'test': 'Two-prop z',
                     'statistic': r['z_stat'], 'p_value': r['p_value'],
                     'reject_H0': r['reject_H0']})

    for col in categorical_cols:
        sub = df[df[group_col].isin([group_a, group_b])]
        r = test_categorical_association(sub, group_col, col, alpha=alpha)
        rows.append({'confounder': col, 'test': 'Chi-square',
                     'statistic': r['chi2'], 'p_value': r['p_value'],
                     'reject_H0': r['reject_H0']})

    return pd.DataFrame(rows)


# Build candidate confounder lists by dtype
confounders = confounder_panel(
    merged_df,
    group_col='cluster',
    group_a=HIGH_RISK_CLUSTER,
    group_b=LOW_RISK_CLUSTER,
    continuous_cols=['age', 'comorbidity_count', 'length_of_stay_days'],
    binary_cols=['gender'],
    categorical_cols=['age_group'],
)

Key Findings:

  • age (continuous), comorbidity_count (continuous), and age_group (categorical) are identified as significant confounders. Their p_value is effectively 0 and reject_H0 is True. This is expected, as these variables were used to define our risk strata (charlson_index and age). They significantly differ between the high-risk and low-risk groups.

  • length_of_stay_days and gender are not identified as confounders. Their p_value is high (0.8037 and 0.6960, respectively) and reject_H0 is False. This means there's no statistically significant difference in length of stay or gender distribution between the high-risk and low-risk groups.

Implication: Since age and comorbidity are significant confounders, it means that the differences we observe in readmission rates between the high-risk and low-risk groups are, at least in part, due to these underlying demographic and health differences. This doesn't invalidate the primary findings, but it highlights that any interventions based on these risk strata should consider the varying age and comorbidity profiles. The next step, stratified analysis, is designed to investigate this further by re-running the tests within different comorbidity_count categories.

7.5 Stratified confirmation¶

Here, we approach confounder handling by stratifying on the candidate confounder and re-running the primary test inside each stratum. If the effect persists in every stratum, the confounder is not driving the result. If it disappears or flips inside strata, we had a confounded comparison (a Simpson's paradox style outcome).

In [75]:
def stratified_test(df, outcome_col, group_col, group_a, group_b, stratify_col,
                    outcome_type='continuous', alpha=0.05):
    """Run the primary test within each level of stratify_col.

    outcome_type='continuous' -> Welch t-test on outcome_col means.
    outcome_type='binary'     -> two-proportion z-test on outcome_col rates.
    """
    rows = []
    for level, sub in df.groupby(stratify_col):
        a = sub[sub[group_col] == group_a][outcome_col]
        b = sub[sub[group_col] == group_b][outcome_col]
        if len(a) < 2 or len(b) < 2:
            continue   # skip strata with too few rows for inference
        if outcome_type == 'continuous':
            r = test_means(a, b, alpha=alpha)
            rows.append({'stratum': level, 'n_a': r['n_a'], 'n_b': r['n_b'],
                         'mean_diff': r['mean_diff'], 'p_value': r['p_value'],
                         'reject_H0': r['reject_H0']})
        else:
            r = test_proportions(int(a.sum()), len(a), int(b.sum()), len(b), alpha=alpha)
            rows.append({'stratum': level, 'n_a': r['n_a'], 'n_b': r['n_b'],
                         'risk_diff': r['risk_diff'], 'p_value': r['p_value'],
                         'reject_H0': r['reject_H0']})
    return pd.DataFrame(rows)

Interpreting the stratified results. Both A/B tests from Sections 7.2 and 7.3 survive the stratification check on comorbidity_count, the confounder identified as significantly different between risk strata in 7.4 (Welch's t-test, p ≈ 3.2e-232). The two tests survive in different ways: the cost null finding reproduces with mixed evidence across strata, and the readmission effect reproduces with the same direction in every stratum.

Cost stratified by comorbidity_count (table strat_cost):

  • 1 dx (stratum 1): n_high = 23, n_low = 142, mean_diff = -$2,082.71, p = 0.3777. Fails to reject.
  • 2 dx (stratum 2): n_high = 125, n_low = 221, mean_diff = -$177.12, p = 0.9278. Fails to reject.
  • 3 dx (stratum 3): n_high = 402, n_low = 165, mean_diff = +$3,081.21, p = 0.0365. Rejects.
  • 4 dx (stratum 4): n_high = 740, n_low = 72, mean_diff = +$787.96, p = 0.6744. Fails to reject.
  • 5 dx (stratum 5): n_high = 669, n_low = 22, mean_diff = +$3,781.75, p = 0.0535. Borderline, fails to reject.
  • 6 dx (stratum 6): n_high = 364, n_low = 4, mean_diff = -$20,507.93, p = 0.2336. Fails to reject (n_low = 4 too small).

The unstratified non-finding (p = 0.148, mean_diff = $1,008.60, Cohen's d = 0.059) is broadly preserved: 5 of the 6 strata fail to reject, and the one significant stratum (3 dx) is bracketed by non-significant ones in both directions. The mean-difference signs are mixed (negative at 1, 2, and 6 dx; positive at 3, 4, and 5 dx), and the negative-direction strata are precisely the ones with very imbalanced sample sizes (n_high = 23 at 1 dx; n_low = 4 at 6 dx). This is the expected pattern when stratifying on a variable that is itself strongly correlated with the High vs Low risk rule: the rule embeds Charlson, which is a weighted comorbidity score, so extreme values of comorbidity_count produce strata that are dominated by one group or the other. There is no Simpson's paradox lurking that would overturn the unstratified non-effect; the data simply does not support a population-level cost gap in any robust way.

Readmission stratified by comorbidity_count (table strat_readmit):

  • 1 dx: n_high = 23, n_low = 142, risk_diff = 0.0588 (5.88 pp), p = 0.1624. Fails to reject.
  • 2 dx: n_high = 125, n_low = 221, risk_diff = 0.1332 (13.32 pp), p = 0.000118. Rejects.
  • 3 dx: n_high = 402, n_low = 165, risk_diff = 0.0904 (9.04 pp), p = 0.00522. Rejects.
  • 4 dx: n_high = 740, n_low = 72, risk_diff = 0.0659 (6.59 pp), p = 0.156. Fails to reject.
  • 5 dx: n_high = 669, n_low = 22, risk_diff = 0.2123 (21.23 pp), p = 0.0153. Rejects.
  • 6 dx: n_high = 364, n_low = 4, risk_diff = 0.2253 (22.53 pp), p = 0.282. Fails to reject (n_low = 4 too small).

The risk_diff is positive in every single stratum (High group readmission > Low group readmission), ranging from 5.88 pp to 22.53 pp and bracketing the unstratified 14.15 pp gap from 7.3. Three of the six strata individually reject the null at α = 0.05. Of the three that fail to reject, each has a limiting sample size that constrains power: stratum 1 has only n_high = 23, stratum 4 has n_low = 72, and stratum 6 has n_low = 4. The non-rejections are therefore better explained by reduced statistical power in imbalanced or low-count strata than by a genuinely absent effect, especially since the observed risk_diff is positive in all three (5.88 pp, 6.59 pp, and 22.53 pp respectively). Even after we strip out the variance attributable to comorbidity_count, the High-risk segment is more likely to be readmitted at every level of overall comorbidity burden. The signal is being driven by the combination of Charlson severity and age that defines risk_stratum, not by the raw count of conditions.

Combined conclusion: Stratifying on comorbidity_count reproduces both findings from the unstratified analysis. The cost test continues to point to no robust population-level gap (5 of 6 strata fail to reject, the lone rejection at 3 dx is isolated, and the negative-direction strata are explained by small-sample artifacts). The readmission test continues to point to a strong and consistent High-risk effect (positive risk_diff in every stratum, three rejections, and the non-rejections explained by reduced statistical power from imbalanced or low-count strata). The business recommendation from Section 9 (target the High-risk stratum with a readmission-reduction intervention) is therefore robust to controlling for comorbidity burden, the confounder that the 7.4 panel identified as significantly different between strata, and can be made at the population level rather than restricted to a particular comorbidity tier.

7.6 Tradeoffs to consider¶

  • T-test vs Mann-Whitney: t-test is more powerful when the sampling distribution of the mean is approximately normal (CLT applies for n above ~30), Mann-Whitney is more robust to skew. Cost is right-skewed, so the t-test result should be cross-checked with mannwhitneyu for robustness.
  • Two-proportion z-test vs chi-square: equivalent for a 2 x 2 table; chi-square generalizes to larger contingency tables.
  • Multiple-testing concern: running several tests inflates the family-wise error rate. Across Sections 7.2–7.5 we run roughly 20 hypothesis tests (the two primary tests plus the one-sided variant, the 5-row confounder panel, and the 12 stratified comparisons). Under Bonferroni at alpha / 20 = 0.0025, only the readmission rejection (p ≋ 0) survives. The cost-related p-values would fail under any reasonable correction, which is consistent with our null finding for cost.
  • Statistical significance is not clinical significance. Always report effect size (Cohen's d for means, risk difference for proportions) alongside the p-value.
  • These tests identify confounders; they do not correct for them. Formal correction requires stratification or regression adjustment.

8. Simulation: Bootstrap and Monte Carlo¶

Why simulation: point estimates hide uncertainty. A single sample mean is one realization of a random variable; the bootstrap builds the empirical sampling distribution of that statistic by resampling the observed data with replacement, and we read a 95% confidence interval off the percentiles of that distribution. Monte Carlo simulation, in this context, simulates forward (what could next year's revenue look like).

Course conventions we follow:

  • Random source: np.random.default_rng(seed=RANDOM_SEED).
  • Resampling: rng.choice(data, size=len(data), replace=True).
  • Iteration count: 5,000 by default (the convention used in both the Bootstrap and Monte Carlo course notebooks).
  • CI extraction: np.percentile([2.5, 97.5]) for a 95% percentile CI.

8.1 Generic bootstrap helper¶

In [77]:
def bootstrap_metric(data, stat_func=np.mean, n_iter=5000, seed=RANDOM_SEED):
    """Resample data with replacement n_iter times, applying stat_func each time.

    Returns
    -------
    numpy.ndarray of length n_iter containing the statistic for each resample.
    Use np.percentile(result, [2.5, 97.5]) to get a 95% percentile CI.
    """
    rng_local = np.random.default_rng(seed=seed)
    data = np.asarray(data)
    out = np.empty(n_iter)
    for i in range(n_iter):
        sample = rng_local.choice(data, size=len(data), replace=True)
        out[i] = stat_func(sample)
    return out


def plot_bootstrap(boot_dist, ci, title, xlabel):
    """Histogram with vertical lines at the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles."""
    plt.figure(figsize=(9, 4))
    sns.histplot(boot_dist, kde=True, color='steelblue')
    plt.axvline(ci[0], color='red', linestyle='--', label=f'2.5%: {ci[0]:,.2f}')
    plt.axvline(ci[1], color='red', linestyle='--', label=f'97.5%: {ci[1]:,.2f}')
    plt.title(title)
    plt.xlabel(xlabel)
    plt.ylabel('Frequency')
    plt.legend()
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()

8.2 Bootstrap the mean total cost¶

In [78]:
# Resample total_charges_usd 5,000 times and compute the mean for each resample.

ci_mean_cost = np.percentile(boot_mean_cost, [2.5, 97.5])

Observed mean cost:       $18,324.52
Bootstrap 95% CI for mean cost: [$17,924.05, $18,731.15]

Interpreting the bootstrap of mean total cost.

The observed mean cost is $18,324.52 and the bootstrap 95% CI is [$17,924.05, $18,731.15]. The CI is tight (roughly $400 on either side of the point estimate, about 2.2% relative to the mean), which is the expected behavior when the sample is large (~6,725 stays after the data quality filter) and the bootstrap is doing its job of giving us a sharp picture of where the population mean cost likely sits. For budgeting purposes, leadership should plan against the upper bound ( around $18,731 per admission) rather than the point estimate, both as a precaution and as a hedge against the right-skew in the cost distribution that the mean already partly absorbs.

8.3 Bootstrap the 30-day readmission rate¶

In [79]:

Bootstrap 95% CI:            [0.1396, 0.1560]

Interpreting the bootstrap of the 30-day readmission rate.

The observed readmission rate is 14.80% with a 95% CI of [13.96%, 15.60%]. The CI is narrow (about 0.8 percentage points on each side), again a function of the large sample size. The upper bound matters operationally: capacity planning for readmission-related care should assume up to ~15.6% of all admissions return within 30 days, not just the point estimate. Note also that the entire CI sits well above CMS national benchmarks (which hover around 13 to 15% for most adult DRGs), suggesting this synthetic hospital's overall readmission performance is near or slightly above the national average even before we stratify by risk.

8.4 Bootstrap the difference in mean cost between two clusters¶

In [80]:
def bootstrap_diff_means(group_a, group_b, n_iter=5000, seed=RANDOM_SEED):
    """Bootstrap the difference in means (a minus b).

    Each iteration resamples within each group, computes its mean, and stores the
    difference. The result is the empirical sampling distribution of the mean diff.
    """
    rng_local = np.random.default_rng(seed=seed)
    a = np.asarray(group_a)
    b = np.asarray(group_b)
    out = np.empty(n_iter)
    for i in range(n_iter):
        out[i] = (rng_local.choice(a, size=len(a), replace=True).mean() -
                  rng_local.choice(b, size=len(b), replace=True).mean())
    return out


# Re-use the same high/low risk cluster arrays from Section 7
boot_diff = bootstrap_diff_means(cost_high, cost_low)
ci_diff = np.percentile(boot_diff, [2.5, 97.5])
print(f'Observed mean cost difference: ${(cost_high.mean() - cost_low.mean()):,.2f}')
print(f'Bootstrap 95% CI for the difference: [${ci_diff[0]:,.2f}, ${ci_diff[1]:,.2f}]')

plot_bootstrap(boot_diff, ci_diff,
               'Bootstrap distribution of mean cost difference: high-risk minus low-risk',
               'Cost difference (USD)')

Observed mean cost difference: $1,008.60
Bootstrap 95% CI for the difference: [$-412.18, $2,357.64]

Interpreting the bootstrap of the cost difference, and cross-checking the A/B test.

The observed mean cost difference between High and Low risk strata is $1,008.60. The bootstrap 95% CI on that difference is [-$412.18, $2,357.64], and crucially the interval includes zero.

This is exactly consistent with the Welch's t-test in Section 7.2 failing to reject H0 (two-sided p = 0.148). The CI tells us more than the p-value does: the plausible range of the true mean cost difference runs from a small negative gap (Low-risk group could actually be costlier by up to $400) to a moderately positive gap of about $2,400. There is no statistical case here for High-risk patients having structurally higher per-stay charges.

Business implication: chronic risk (age + comorbidity) does not predict per-admission cost in this dataset. Cost per stay appears to not be driven by the patient's underlying chronic risk profile, but rather the acuity of the episode (DRG, procedure, ICU exposure). This aligns with what PCA showed in Section 5.7, where the cost axis (PC3) loaded negatively on comorbidity_count, suggesting the highest-cost stays are acute single-episode admissions rather than chronic-disease driven stays.

The readmission test in Section 7.3 is where the High-risk signal lives: the bootstrap on readmission rate combined with the 14.15 percentage-point gap from the z-test means the High-risk segment is more than 3 times as likely to return within 30 days as the Low-risk segment. That, not per-stay cost, is the lever for an intervention program.

8.5 Monte Carlo: project forward to next year¶

Suppose hospital volume grows by 10% next year. We simulate 7,500 new admissions (~6,820 x 1.1) by resampling total_charges_usd with replacement, sum to get a single simulated annual revenue, and repeat 5,000 times. The 95% CI on the resulting distribution is leadership's projected revenue band under the assumption that the cost distribution stays the same.

In [81]:
# Monte Carlo forward projection
N_NEW_ADMISSIONS = 7500
N_SIMS = 5000

observed_costs = merged_df['total_charges_usd'].values

total_revenue_sims = np.empty(N_SIMS)
for i in range(N_SIMS):
    simulated_year = rng.choice(observed_costs, size=N_NEW_ADMISSIONS, replace=True)
    total_revenue_sims[i] = simulated_year.sum()

ci_revenue = np.percentile(total_revenue_sims, [2.5, 97.5])
print(f'Mean projected annual revenue: ${total_revenue_sims.mean():,.0f}')
print(f'95% CI: [${ci_revenue[0]:,.0f}, ${ci_revenue[1]:,.0f}]')

plot_bootstrap(total_revenue_sims, ci_revenue,
               f'Monte Carlo: projected annual revenue across {N_SIMS} simulations',
               'Total annual revenue (USD)')

Mean projected annual revenue: $137,421,754
95% CI: [$134,560,881, $140,399,038]
In [82]:
# Closed-form sanity check: expected revenue = N x mean cost per admission.
# Simulation mean should be very close to this analytical value.
analytical_mean_revenue = N_NEW_ADMISSIONS * merged_df['total_charges_usd'].mean()
print(f'Analytical mean revenue (N x mean): ${analytical_mean_revenue:,.0f}')
print(f'Simulation mean revenue:            ${total_revenue_sims.mean():,.0f}')
print(f'Relative difference: {(total_revenue_sims.mean() - analytical_mean_revenue) / analytical_mean_revenue:.4%}')

Analytical mean revenue (N x mean): $137,433,886
Simulation mean revenue:            $137,421,754
Relative difference: -0.0088%

Interpreting the Monte Carlo projection.

The simulation projects mean annual revenue of $137.42M with a 95% CI of [$134.56M, $140.40M] under a 10% volume growth scenario for next year (7,500 admissions). The closed-form sanity check (N times observed mean) yields $137.43M, a relative difference of about 0.01%, which confirms the simulation is converging correctly and not introducing a systematic bias.

Decision-useful framing for leadership:

  • Budget against the lower bound: at the 2.5th percentile, revenue could come in as low as $134.56M, about $3M below the point estimate. Reserves should reflect this.
  • Plan capital expenditure against the upper bound: at the 97.5th percentile, revenue could be as high as $140.40M, which is the realistic ceiling for next year under a no-regime-change assumption.
  • The total spread (~$5.8M, or about 4.2% of the mean) is the year-over-year variability driven purely by case mix randomness, before any operational changes or rate negotiations.
In [83]:
# Parametric variant: fit a lognormal to total_charges_usd (right-skewed) and draw
# from that fit instead of empirical resampling. Compare CIs to test sensitivity
# to the distribution choice.
log_costs = np.log(observed_costs)
mu_log = log_costs.mean()
sigma_log = log_costs.std(ddof=1)

parametric_revenue_sims = np.empty(N_SIMS)
for i in range(N_SIMS):
    draws = np.exp(rng.normal(mu_log, sigma_log, size=N_NEW_ADMISSIONS))
    draws = np.clip(draws, a_min=0, a_max=None)   # enforce non-negative
    parametric_revenue_sims[i] = draws.sum()

ci_parametric = np.percentile(parametric_revenue_sims, [2.5, 97.5])
print(f'Empirical-resample 95% CI: [${ci_revenue[0]:,.0f}, ${ci_revenue[1]:,.0f}]')
print(f'Parametric (lognormal) CI: [${ci_parametric[0]:,.0f}, ${ci_parametric[1]:,.0f}]')

Empirical-resample 95% CI: [$134,560,881, $140,399,038]
Parametric (lognormal) CI: [$134,065,549, $139,773,860]

Interpreting the empirical vs parametric comparison.

The empirical-resample CI is [$134.56M, $140.40M] and the parametric lognormal CI is [$134.07M, $139.77M]. The two intervals overlap almost completely (the bounds differ by less than 0.5% on either side), which tells us two related things:

  1. The cost distribution is well-approximated by a lognormal. The right skew we saw in the descriptive statistics in Section 2 is captured by exp(Normal(mu_log, sigma_log)), and once you draw from that fit and apply np.clip(>=0), you get essentially the same distribution as the empirical observations.
  2. The Monte Carlo projection is distribution-robust at this sample size. Whether we trust the empirical sample or a parametric fit, we land on the same revenue band. Leadership can therefore treat the headline CI ($134.6M to $140.4M) as a reasonably trustworthy projection rather than an artifact of one resampling choice.

In finance terms, this is the analytical version of "the model survives an obvious robustness check." If the two CIs had diverged sharply, that would have been a sign the lognormal fit was poor in the tails and the empirical resample was the safer of the two.

8.6 Tradeoffs to consider¶

  • Bootstrap assumes the observed sample is representative of the population. Sampling bias propagates into the CI.
  • Bootstrap cannot extrapolate beyond the observed range; it underestimates extreme tail percentiles (e.g., the maximum).
  • Bootstrap especially shines for bounded parameters (proportions near 0 or 1, percentiles, ratios) where normal approximation fails.
  • Monte Carlo here is a trend-continues projection; it ignores regime changes such as new reimbursement rules or demographic shifts. Scenario analysis is the standard extension.
  • Parametric Monte Carlo requires picking a distribution; misspecification biases the result. Empirical resampling avoids that but cannot generate values outside the observed range.

9. Conclusions and Business Recommendations¶

This analysis chained five techniques together and produced one important diagnostic finding about the dataset itself along the way.

1. Data screening and feature engineering. We flagged 1,251 rows at the source level (1,200 BP-impossible in patient_df and 51 ICU-impossible in outcome_df). After the left-join from outcomes onto patients, 95 of the 6,820 stays inherited a quality flag and were excluded, leaving 6,725 clean hospital stays in the analytical dataset. We engineered seven new features (comorbidity_count, pulse_pressure, age_group, bp_category, bmi_category, daily_charge, high_cost_flag) that translate raw EHR fields into clinically interpretable risk and cost indicators.

2. PCA returned a diagnostic, not a compression. Bartlett's test rejected the identity null (chi-square = 250,410, p = 0), but KMO came in at 0.511 (miserable band). The Kaiser rule retained 7 components for only 69.04% cumulative variance, with the scree elbow falling around PC4 at ~47% variance. This is what an essentially uncorrelated feature space looks like; the synthetic generator drew most patient features independently, leaving little shared variance for PCA to consolidate.

3. K-Means inherited the weakness. Silhouette peaked at k = 3 with a score of 0.143 (problematic band, below 0.25). The resulting partition mostly recovered the engineered high_cost_flag rather than discovering distinct patient personas: Cluster 2 was essentially the high-cost stays (mean $58,953, 100% high_cost_flag), while Clusters 0 and 1 differed in age and comorbidity but were nearly identical in cost and outcomes.

4. Pivot to a clinically-defined segmentation. We stratified patients into Low, Medium, and High risk using the rule (charlson_index >= 2) AND (age >= 65) for High, and the inverse for Low. The resulting strata produce a clean monotonic gradient on every clinically meaningful row of the profile heatmap: age (51 to 78 to 84), comorbidity_count (2.2 to 3.3 to 4.5), charlson_index (0.42 to 0.72 to 2.49), systolic_bp, diastolic_bp, pulse_pressure, and crucially the outcome rows.

5. A/B testing produced two findings of opposite character.

  • Cost per Stay (Welch's t-test): the mean cost difference between High and Low risk strata is only $1,008.60 (mean_a = $18,673, mean_b = $17,665), with a two-sided p = 0.148, a one-sided p = 0.074, and a Cohen's d of just 0.059. We fail to reject the null. We cannot conclude that there's a statistically significant difference in costs between High and Low risk groups.
  • Readmission (two-proportion z-test): the 30-day readmission rate is 5.74% in Low and 19.89% in High, a 14.15 percentage point risk difference and a 3.5x relative risk (0.1989 / 0.0574 = 3.47), with z = 8.74 and p ~ 0. We strongly reject the null, so the readmission rate for the High risk group is significantly higher than that of the Low risk group. Chronic risk is the dominant driver of who returns within 30 days.
  • Confounder panel: age and comorbidity_count differ between strata by construction (Welch t p ~ 0). Length of stay and gender do not differ between strata (p = 0.804 and p = 0.696). To control for the comorbidity confounder identified above, Section 7.5 re-runs both primary tests within each level of comorbidity_count. The readmission risk_diff stays positive in every stratum (5.9 pp to 22.5 pp) with three of six strata individually rejecting, while the cost test continues to point to no robust gap (5 of 6 strata fail to reject). Both unstratified findings survive.

6. Bootstrap and Monte Carlo simulation quantified the uncertainty.

  • 95% CI on mean cost: [$17,924, $18,731], width about $800.
  • 95% CI on readmission rate: [13.96%, 15.60%], width about 1.6 percentage points.
  • 95% CI on the cost difference between High and Low risk groups: [-$412, +$2,358]. The interval includes zero, which confirms the t-test finding: there is no significant, positive cost gap.
  • 95% CI on next year's projected revenue (10% volume growth, 7,500 admissions): [$134.6M, $140.4M] around a mean of $137.4M. The closed-form analytical mean ($137.43M) matches the simulation mean to 0.01%. The parametric lognormal CI ($134.1M to $139.8M) overlaps the empirical CI to within ~0.5%, confirming the cost distribution is well-approximated by a lognormal and the projection is robust to the distributional assumption.

Practical recommendation. The actionable lever is readmission, not cost. A care-transition or chronic-disease management program targeting the High-risk stratum can plausibly move the readmission rate by a few percentage points; even a 2-percentage-point reduction in the High stratum applied to the 2,484 High-risk admissions per year would prevent roughly 50 readmissions annually, as well as preventing those associated downstream costs. The per-stay cost difference, by contrast, is not a useful target because it does not exist as a statistically meaningful gap in this data.

Limitations and lessons.

  • The dataset is synthetic and the features were drawn approximately independently, which suppresses the correlations PCA and K-Means need to work. A real-world EHR cohort would likely yield a stronger unsupervised pipeline.
  • We identified confounders but did not formally control for them. Regression adjustment (or matched-pair design) is the next step for any causal claim.
  • The Monte Carlo projection assumes the cost distribution stays the same year over year; regime changes (new reimbursement rules, demographic shifts, payer mix changes) are not modeled.
  • The honest reporting of the KMO and silhouette diagnostics is itself a relevant finding. Choosing techniques that fit the data, and pivoting away from techniques that do not, is better than forcing clusters with a poor silhouette score.
